title: Get ready for 3 consecutive rate hikes starting next month, bank warns
summary:
A hat trick of Federal Reserve rate hikes is on the way, BNP Paribas says.
That would put the fed funds rate at 4.5%-4.75%, up from its 3.75%-4% range.
"We believe the FOMC, in its three upcoming meetings, will remove three more doses of accommodation," Egelhof wrote.
BNP said the economy has not cooled sufficiently following the Fed's September rate hike and that further tightening is needed.
However, while the labor market could prove durable enough to withstand a few hikes, AI stocks could suffer from such an outcome, BNP said.

title: Nepal PM Balendra Shah visit: India to give $1.62bn economic package
summary:
A Hindu-majority nation wedged between India and China, Nepal has long had to navigate competing interests from its two giant neighbours.
As a landlocked country heavily dependent on India for trade, Nepal secured access to two additional Indian ports, Kandla and Paradip.
Nepal has long sought greater access to Indian airspace in order to attract international traffic to its airports at Bhairahawa and Pokhara.
Shah must now manage relations with China as he seeks to balance the interests of Nepal's two much larger neighbours.
For now he returns home with substantial financial commitments from India as Nepal continues the long task of rebuilding.

title: Countries that thrive on global cooperation must help sustain it
summary:
“For thriving states, international peace and stability are not a luxury.
The prime minister’s concept of thriving states offers a way to think about their response.
The Global North and the Global South tell us little about which countries can work together on a particular problem.
Their diplomatic access and financial resources are increasingly necessary to sustain functions that international institutions struggle to perform consistently.
The next step is to organise sustained cooperation among willing thriving states.

title: How the US, China and Russia are competing for Africa’s mineral wealth
summary:
The US, China and Russia are vying for Africa’s mineral wealth, raising questions about who stands to benefitShare How the US, China and Russia are competing for Africa’s mineral wealth on social mediaFrom cobalt mines in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to lithium deposits in Mali and uranium reserves in Niger, Africa’s mineral wealth is becoming an increasingly important arena of competition between the United States, China and Russia.
China dominates several critical mineral supply chains, while Russia has expanded its influence through security partnerships, particularly in the Sahel.
But as foreign powers compete for access, what do African countries stand to gain?
China has spent years investing in African mining, processing and infrastructure.
As Washington, Beijing and Moscow compete for Africa’s mineral wealth, the real test for African countries may be not which global power wins the race, but how much of the wealth they can retain.
